---
title: "Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions"
---

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed
frequencies. A model assigning 0.02 to many ad impressions should see clicks on
about 2% of them. A model reporting 0.8 probability that its answer is correct
should be right on about 80% of comparable predictions.

This note covers post-hoc calibration, advertising-specific data problems, and
calibration-oriented language-model training. The recent-work discussion was
checked on **October 5, 2026**. Jev's RLCD is treated as a publicly stated
objective; its undisclosed implementation is not reconstructed from related
papers.

## Define the Probability Before Calibrating It

For a binary outcome $Y$ and prediction $p(X)$, population calibration means

$$
\mathbb E[Y\mid p(X)=s]=s.
$$

In finite data, estimate this using groups of nearby predictions. Calibration
is a property of a predictor **on a distribution**, not a certificate that an
individual prediction is correct.

| Setting | Probability being estimated | Relevant evaluation population |
|---|---|---|
| CTR | $P(C=1\mid X)$ | Served impressions |
| Post-click CVR | $P(V_H=1\mid C=1,X)$ | Clicked impressions, with conversion horizon $H$ |
| Click-through conversion rate | $P(C=1,V_H=1\mid X)$ | Served impressions |
| Multiclass prediction | $P(Y=k\mid X)$ for each class | Labeled examples from the target population |
| Answer confidence | $P(\text{answer is correct}\mid X,\text{answer},\text{available evidence})$ | Answers generated by the deployed model and decoding procedure |

A constant predictor equal to the population base rate can be calibrated but
useless for ranking. Conversely, a strictly increasing transformation can
preserve ranking while damaging probabilities. Calibration, discrimination,
and decision quality therefore need separate evaluation.

For multiclass models, **top-label calibration** checks confidence in the
selected class. **Classwise calibration** checks each class probability.
Neither should be silently substituted for calibration of the entire
probability vector.

## Proper Scoring Rules: Why CE and Brier Are Natural Baselines

A loss is strictly proper if its expected value is uniquely minimized by the
true outcome distribution. Two binary examples are

$$
\ell_{\log}(p,y)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p),
\qquad
\ell_{\mathrm{Brier}}(p,y)=(p-y)^2.
$$

If $Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)$, then

$$
\mathbb E[(p-Y)^2]=(p-q)^2+q(1-q),
$$

so the optimum is $p=q$. For log loss, the excess expected loss above the
optimum is $\operatorname{KL}(\operatorname{Bern}(q)\|\operatorname{Bern}(p))$.
This connects calibration to [cross-entropy and distillation](distillation.qmd).
See [Gneiting and Raftery (2007), Strictly Proper Scoring Rules](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf).

Training with CE already has the right population target. Finite data,
restricted model capacity, regularization, optimization, and train/serve
mismatch can still produce miscalibration. A proper objective is an incentive,
not a finite-sample guarantee. Brier and NLL also measure predictive quality
beyond calibration, so neither is a pure calibration-error metric.

## Classical Post-Hoc Methods

Freeze the base predictor. Fit a small mapping on a **separate calibration
set**, then evaluate it on untouched test data. Here $z$ is a raw binary score
or logit, $p$ is an existing probability, and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid.

| Method | Mapping or fit | Useful regime and limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Intercept correction | $\sigma(z+b)$ | Correct a probability-level offset under an appropriate shift model; cannot fix arbitrary shape errors |
| Platt/logistic scaling | $\sigma(az+b)$ | Low-variance baseline; $a>0$ preserves ranking, but a sigmoid may be too restrictive |
| Temperature scaling | $\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)$, $T>0$ | One parameter for multiclass logits; preserves the selected class, cannot correct class-specific biases |
| Histogram binning | Replace each bin by its empirical positive rate | Simple diagnostic and baseline; sensitive to bins and sparse counts, not necessarily monotone |
| Isotonic regression | Fit a nondecreasing map minimizing squared error | Flexible scalar correction; needs sufficient data and introduces ties |
| Beta calibration | $\sigma(a\log p-b\log(1-p)+c)$ | Flexible correction for asymmetric probability distortion; $a,b\geq0$ ensure monotonicity |

Platt scaling and isotonic regression are compared in
[Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (ICML 2005)](https://icml.cc/Conferences/2005/proceedings/papers/079_GoodProbabilities_NiculescuMizilCaruana.pdf).
Fit their parameters using held-out predictions, not the predictions on which
the base model was trained.

[Guo et al. (ICML 2017)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html)
find temperature scaling effective on their neural-network benchmarks. It
fits $T$ by minimizing calibration-set NLL. For a binary logit this becomes
$\sigma(z/T)$; the missing intercept matters when the problem is a changed
base rate rather than excessive sharpness.

[Beta calibration (AISTATS 2017)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v54/kull17a.html)
includes the identity mapping at $a=b=1,c=0$. This distinguishes it from
fitting $\sigma(ap+b)$ directly to probabilities. Clip inputs away from 0 and
1 for numerical stability. A multiclass extension is
[Dirichlet calibration (NeurIPS 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.12656),
which transforms log probabilities with a learned linear map followed by
softmax; its extra parameters require regularization and more calibration data.

## CTR/CVR: Correct the Data-Generating Problem First

### Negative downsampling and weighted BCE

Suppose all positive examples are kept, while negatives are retained with
probability $s$. Let $p_s$ be the posterior in the sampled population. Bayes'
rule gives the production posterior

$$
p=\frac{s p_s}{1-p_s+s p_s},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p)=\operatorname{logit}(p_s)+\log s.
$$

For $s=0.1$ and $p_s=0.2$, the corrected probability is about $0.0244$, not
$0.02$: multiplying by $s$ is only a small-probability approximation.
[He et al., Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook
(ADKDD 2014), §6.3](https://www.quinonero.net/Publications/predicting-clicks-facebook.pdf)
describes this recalibration after negative downsampling.

The formula assumes class-dependent sampling with the stated retention rates
and an accurate sampled posterior. Feature-dependent sampling requires the
corresponding conditional rates. Do not apply the correction twice if loss
weights or an existing calibrator already restore the target population.

A related derivation: weighted BCE with positive and negative weights
$w_1,w_0$ has pointwise optimum

$$
p_w=\frac{w_1q}{w_1q+w_0(1-q)},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(q)=\operatorname{logit}(p_w)-\log\frac{w_1}{w_0}.
$$

Thus class weighting changes what the raw output estimates. Record sampling
and weighting choices before interpreting a score as CTR or CVR.

### Delayed conversions and label maturity

Define conversion within a particular horizon $H$. A click from one hour ago
with no conversion is not yet a known negative for seven-day conversion.
Fitting a calibrator on such provisional zeros calibrates toward the wrong
observed target.

Use fully matured labels for the chosen horizon, or explicitly model delay
and censoring when freshness requires partially observed data.
[Chapelle, Modeling Delayed Feedback in Display Advertising (KDD 2014)](https://wnzhang.net/share/rtb-papers/delayed-feedback.pdf)
models both conversion probability and conversion delay. A downstream sigmoid
cannot by itself repair incorrect labels.

### CVR selection and the probability product

For click-attributed conversions,

$$
P(C=1,V_H=1\mid X)
=P(C=1\mid X)P(V_H=1\mid C=1,X).
$$

[ESMM (SIGIR 2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.07931)
uses this structure to jointly learn CTR and click-through conversion on the
impression space, addressing clicked-only training and sparse conversion data.
It is a modeling approach, not a post-hoc calibration guarantee.

Evaluate CVR on the relevant clicked population and the joint probability on
impressions. Even if two component scores each pass marginal reliability
checks, their product need not be calibrated: those checks do not establish
that both scores equal the required conditional probabilities. Avoid treating
logged CVR as a causal conversion probability under an arbitrary new serving
policy.

### Field-aware calibration

Overall bias can hide opposite errors across campaigns, placements, devices,
or countries. For a slice $g$, a useful aggregate diagnostic is

$$
\mathrm{P/O}_g=\frac{\sum_{i\in g}p_i}{\sum_{i\in g}y_i}.
$$

Here values above one mean overprediction. This ratio is undefined with no
observed positives and unstable with very few; report counts and uncertainty.
A ratio near one does not imply calibration within the slice's score bins.

[Pan et al., Field-aware Calibration (WWW 2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10713)
introduces field-level calibration metrics and a neural calibrator of the form

$$
p_{\mathrm{cal}}(x)=\sigma\big(\eta(z(x))+g(x)\big),
$$

combining a scalar logit transformation with a feature-dependent correction,
fitted by log loss on development data. Because features affect the mapping,
it can change ranking across examples. Check both ranking and calibration;
regularize sparse fields instead of fitting an unconstrained map per tiny
segment.

## Evaluation and a Practical Fitting Workflow

For bins $B_b$, binary expected calibration error is commonly estimated as

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}
=\sum_b\frac{|B_b|}{n}\left|
\frac{1}{|B_b|}\sum_{i\in B_b}p_i
-\frac{1}{|B_b|}\sum_{i\in B_b}y_i
\right|.
$$

For top-label ECE, replace $p_i$ with maximum class probability and $y_i$ with
the indicator that the selected class is correct. State which definition you
use. Bin choices and whether all classes are evaluated can change conclusions;
see [Nixon et al., Measuring Calibration in Deep Learning (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01685).

Report reliability plots with bin counts, NLL, Brier score, ranking quality,
and domain-specific aggregate bias together. For rare events, a small absolute
ECE can conceal a large relative error; inspect the low-probability region
and important slices. Bootstrap by the relevant independent unit, such as
user or time block, when observations are correlated.

A recommended workflow, synthesizing the methods above:

1. Define the event, horizon, population, and any selection or weighting.
2. Train the predictor; collect predictions on a later calibration window
   with mature labels. Reserve a still-later test window. Keep tuning separate
   from final evaluation, using additional splits or cross-validation.
3. Compare uncalibrated outputs with a simple logistic/temperature baseline,
   then isotonic or beta calibration. Add feature-aware calibration only when
   slice-level evidence and sample size justify it.
4. Select using probability quality and the downstream decision objective,
   not one ECE number. Check rare slices and distribution shifts.
5. Version the predictor and calibrator together. Monitor fresh outcomes and
   refit when their relationship changes; a calibrator fitted before a model
   update need not remain valid afterwards.

For binary actions with false-positive cost $c_{FP}$ and false-negative cost
$c_{FN}$, and zero cost for correct decisions, expected-cost minimization acts
positive when

$$
p>\frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP}+c_{FN}}.
$$

This explains why calibrated probabilities matter beyond AUC. For selective
answering, also measure **risk–coverage**: error rate among accepted answers
versus fraction accepted. Choose an acceptance threshold on validation data,
then report test performance at that fixed threshold. Finding the best
threshold after observing test labels is not a deployment guarantee.

## Language Models: What Exactly Is Being Calibrated?

Token likelihood is the probability of a particular string under the language
model. It is not automatically the probability that the string's claim is
true. Multiple equivalent answers, prompt format, length, and decoding all
complicate that interpretation.

| Approach | Confidence signal | Relevant work |
|---|---|---|
| Train explicit confidence expression | A generated numeric or verbal estimate | [Lin, Hilton, and Evans (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14334) show supervised learning of verbalized uncertainty |
| Ask the model to assess an answer | Probability of a correctness judgment, such as $P(\mathrm{True})$ | [Kadavath et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221) study self-evaluation and knowledge prediction |
| Calibrate a fixed score | Map an answer score to empirical correctness | Apply held-out logistic/isotonic calibration to the deployed answer-generation pipeline |
| Change training incentives | Reward both answering and honest probability reporting | Rewarding Doubt, RLCR, and newer methods below |

Keep the answer generator, prompt, tools, and sampling procedure fixed when
fitting a post-hoc confidence model. Otherwise the correctness event being
predicted changes. A monotone binary calibrator adjusts the numeric scale;
it cannot turn an uninformative ordering of confidence into a useful ranking
of correct versus incorrect answers.

## Jev and RLCD: Public Objective Versus Disclosed Methods

TypeSafe introduced **Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)**
as the training approach behind Jev in its
[September 15, 2026 launch post](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev).
The public material describes typed probabilistic decisions but does not
provide a reproducible reward, optimizer, or complete training recipe. Its
workflow comparisons use reference-model probabilities; agreement with those
references is different from calibration against observed outcomes.

The product's `confidence` field also deserves care:
[TypeSafe's documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence) defines it as a
statistic derived from the returned distribution, with zero at a uniform
distribution and one at complete concentration. It is not itself automatically
the probability that the chosen answer is correct. Evaluate the relevant
returned probabilities against labels, and validate any routing threshold on
your own target tasks.

::: {.callout-note title="Do not infer Jev's algorithm from its name"}
The proper-score objectives below are published related methods, not a claim
about Jev's internal implementation. Also, the earlier
[RLCD: Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12950)
is a different method with the same acronym.
:::

### Rewarding Doubt: a proper score for reported confidence

[Rewarding Doubt (2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02623v2) trains a model to
express confidence alongside its answer using a logarithmic reward. Let
$Z\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether that answer is correct and let $c$ be the
reported probability:

$$
R_{\log}(c,Z)=Z\log c+(1-Z)\log(1-c).
$$

For a fixed answer whose correctness probability is $q$, expected reward is
maximized at $c=q$. This supplies a direct incentive for honest confidence.
It does not imply that arbitrary joint optimization of answers and confidence
will also maximize accuracy: changing the answer changes the event being
scored. Population optimality and empirical calibration must be distinguished.

### RLCR: reward correctness and calibration together

[Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason about Their Uncertainty
(2025; ICLR 2026)](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.16806v2) proposes RLCR, with

$$
R_{\mathrm{RLCR}}(c,Z)=Z-(c-Z)^2.
$$

The first term rewards a correct answer, while the second scores its reported
confidence. Under the paper's idealized model, for an answer with success
probability $q$,

$$
\mathbb E[R]=q-(c-q)^2-q(1-q).
$$

The best report is $c=q$, and the resulting reward is $q^2$, increasing with
answer quality. This makes the two incentives explicit. The theorem concerns
ideal optima; finite-capacity RL with imperfect correctness judgments still
needs held-out evaluation. The reported scalar confidence is different from
a full categorical distribution over all possible answers.

### Recent related work and evidence limits

| Work | Contribution relevant to calibration | How to interpret the evidence |
|---|---|---|
| [Calibrating LLMs with Semantic-level Reward (May 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15588) | CSR scores semantic answer distributions rather than requiring verbalized confidence | A research preprint; semantic grouping and correctness evaluation are part of the measurement pipeline |
| [Scaling with Confidence (July 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01612) | C3RL combines correctness, confidence calibration, and reference-accuracy rewards; uses confidence for adaptive test-time compute | A proposed alternative reward design, not evidence of Jev's recipe |
| [OpenJev-RLCD (September 30, 2026)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38850v1) | Independent implementation: calibrate the answer distribution after a sampled rationale, then reinforce reasoning with a proper-score reward and a KL anchor | Qwen3-1.7B experiments on two reasoning tasks plus an annotator-disagreement setting; a very recent preprint, not an official Jev reproduction |

OpenJev-RLCD separates scoring each rationale's answer distribution from
scoring an average across rationales. For negative Brier score, averaging
distributions adds a variance term relative to averaging their scores, so the
objectives differ. Its reported selective-prediction improvements are limited
to the studied setup; they do not establish universal superiority over
supervised CE plus calibration. See [OpenJev-RLCD, §§3–5](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38850v1).

Independent studies such as [Just Ask Jev (September 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29429)
and [JevAdvBench (September 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31142) evaluate
Jev's behavior and robustness. They are useful application evidence, not
disclosures of its training algorithm or guarantees of target-domain calibration.

## When Is RL Actually Needed?

For a fixed labeled classification problem with a differentiable probability
head, CE or Brier can be optimized directly. Calling negative Brier a reward
does not make policy-gradient training necessary. The classical calibration
baselines should remain part of the comparison.

RL becomes relevant when training must change **sampled reasoning, tool use,
or sequential decisions** that influence the eventual prediction or observed
outcome. Proper scores can supply a calibration incentive, but the choice of
what is scored matters: a full outcome distribution, the correctness of a
selected answer, and success after taking an action are different targets.

For action-dependent outcomes, specify the action and policy in the target
probability. Passive labels collected under an old policy may not identify
success under a new one. For annotator disagreement, decide whether to predict
a majority label or the distribution of judgments; additional reasoning cannot
be assumed to remove disagreement inherent in that target.

## Interview Questions and Exercises

- Why can a base-rate predictor be calibrated but unhelpful?
- Derive negative-downsampling correction and the weighted-BCE optimum.
- Why might temperature scaling fail to correct a shifted CTR base rate?
- Why do calibrated CTR and CVR scores not guarantee a calibrated product?
- How do you evaluate seven-day CVR without treating pending events as negatives?
- Why does a proper score incentivize honest probabilities? What assumptions
  separate that statement from a production guarantee?
- Derive the optimal confidence and answer-quality incentive under RLCR.
- Compare event probability, answer correctness, token likelihood, and Jev's
  distribution-derived confidence statistic.
- Fit logistic, isotonic, and beta calibrators on a chronological split;
  compare NLL, Brier, reliability plots, P/O, and slice-level results.
- Compare CE plus post-hoc calibration with a calibration-reward method using
  the same data and a reported compute budget; evaluate fixed-threshold
  risk–coverage on untouched tasks.
